title: The Gathering of the Confederates
subtitle: Ten Thousand at the Gates: The Coalition Against Madinah
summary: The political incitement by exiled chieftains of Banu al-Nadir, the false religious testimony validating idolatry, the ten-thousand-strong alliance of Quraysh and Ghatafan, the intelligence report to Madinah, and Salman al-Farsi's innovative defense proposal.

sections.text: Following their expulsion from Madinah, the aristocratic leadership of Banu al-Nadir settled in the fortified oasis of Khaybar, approximately ninety miles to the north. Driven by intense resentment, their chieftains—foremost among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and Kinana ibn al-Rabi'—resolved that piecemeal tribal warfare was insufficient to eradicate the Islamic message. They conceived a grand political project: a pan-Arab confederation combining the merchant aristocracy of Makkah, the formidable Bedouin warrior federations of central Arabia, and the resources of northern oases to overwhelm Madinah in a single, devastating campaign.

A high-level delegation of twenty leaders from Banu al-Nadir and Banu Wa'il journeyed south to Makkah. Meeting Abu Sufyan and the elders of Quraysh at the Ka'bah, they pledged full military and financial coordination: 'We shall join our forces with yours until we eradicate Muhammad and his companions entirely.' Seeking theological validation from custodians of ancient scripture, the idolaters asked: 'You are the people of the first Book and possess ancient religious learning; tell us, is our religion better, or is the religion of Muhammad better?'

The classical sirah says the visitors told Quraysh that their religion was better guided than the Prophet's. That sentence is the biography's report of the meeting. Surah al-Nisa 4:51 censures those who were given a share of Scripture and then say of the disbelievers that they are better guided. The verse does not itself name this delegation. Connecting the verse to the meeting is the traditional reading of the occasion, not a line of the verse.

أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا نَصِيبًا مِّنَ الْكِتَابِ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْجِبْتِ وَالطَّاغُوتِ وَيَقُولُونَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا هَٰؤُلَاءِ أَهْدَىٰ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا سَبِيلًا
'Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in superstition and false deities and say about the disbelievers, "These are better guided than the believers as to the way."' (Surah An-Nisa 4:51)
The Alliance in the Classical Account

The classical sirah says the envoys then went to Najd and drew in Ghatafan, including Uyaynah ibn Hisn, with clans of Murrah, Ashja', Sulaym, and Asad. It offers them half the date crop of Khaybar in the telling, and it gives the familiar totals: about a thousand with Uyaynah, and about ten thousand in all, with horses and camels numbered in the hundreds and above a thousand. Those figures are the biography's. The Quran speaks of armies and does not state them. Nor does the sirah establish that this host was larger than every adult in Madinah.

The loyal scouts of the Banu Khuza'ah, riding with astonishing endurance, traversed the desert from Makkah to Madinah in just four days to warn the Prophet ﷺ of the approaching storm. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ immediately convened an emergency council of war (Shura). Traditional pitched battle on the open plains was out of the question; facing an army outnumbering them more than three to one would invite swift encirclement.

Madinah's geography offered natural defensive fortifications on three sides: the sharp, impassable volcanic lava fields of Harrat Waqim to the east, Harrat al-Wabrah to the west, and dense, interconnected palm groves and fortified homesteads to the south. However, the northern expanse lay completely flat and open to cavalry charges. In the council, Salman al-Farsi, the Persian companion whose journey for truth had brought him from Isfahan to Madinah, stepped forward with an unprecedented proposal:

'O Messenger of Allah,' Salman suggested, 'in the land of Persia, when we were besieged by overwhelming cavalry, we used to dig a deep trench (khandaq) around ourselves.' This strategic concept was entirely alien to the norms of Arabian warfare, which relied upon open cavalry skirmishes and tribal charges. The Prophet ﷺ embraced Salman's stratagem with immediate decisiveness, mobilizing the entire community to execute the defense.

references.title: The Holy Quran
references.author: Surah An-Nisa (4:51–52) & Surah Al-Ahzab (33:9–11)
references.notes: The verse censures those given a share of Scripture who say the disbelievers are better guided. Linking it to the Khaybar delegation is the reported occasion, not the verse's own wording.

references.title: Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah
references.author: Ibn Hisham (d. 218 AH), reporting Ibn Ishaq
references.notes: The recruitment of Quraysh, Ghatafan, and the other clans is the classical sirah. Bukhari 4101 is the digging of the trench and Jabir's meal, not this negotiation, so it is not cited for the gathering. The usual sirah total is about ten thousand. The Quran speaks of armies, not of that number.
